extracted.intended_audience: Catholic children and catechism students; general Catholic faithful seeking instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Question-and-answer catechism instruction on angels, the Fall, original and actual sin, the conditions making sin mortal or venial, vocation, and the seven capital sins. Presents definitions, examples, and moral guidance for readers learning doctrine and moral obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angels hierarchy (nine choirs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angels are not all equal in dignity, but are divided into nine classes, or choirs, ... arranged from the lowest to the highest and named as follows; angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names and relative rank are given; archangels are higher than angels and are 'so called because sent to do the most important works.' Examples: Michael and Gabriel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of angels (including guardian angels)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angels were created to assist before the throne of God and to minister unto Him; they have often been sent as messengers from God to man; and are also appointed our guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardian angels: remain with persons night and day, offer our prayers and good works to God, pray for us, exhort us to do good and avoid evil, and protect us from spiritual and temporal dangers. Moral admonition: do not 'impose on him the painful duty of bringing to God the report of your evil doings.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Angels may appear visibly though have no bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The catechism says angels have no bodies--how, then, could they appear? They took bodies made of some very light substance which would make them visible, and appeared just like beautiful young men, clad in flowing garments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains biblical appearances (e.g., Lot, shepherds) as angels assuming visible forms; used as explanatory doctrine for scriptural visions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallen angels / devils: cause and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: All the angels did not remain good and happy; many of them sinned and were cast into Hell; and these are called devils or bad angels. Lucifer (light-bearer) became sinfully proud and wished to be equal to God; for his sin he and all his followers were driven out of Heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains origin of Satan and devils and that Hell was created for their eternal punishment; notes devils may be sent to punish men for sins (example: angel who killed 185,000 in Sennacherib's army).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adam and Eve: creation and original innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: The first man and woman were Adam and Eve. Adam and Eve were innocent and holy when they came from the hand of God. God placed Adam and Eve in Paradise ... Our first parents, in their state of original innocence, were the happy friends of God, without sorrow or suffering of any kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eve was made from Adam's rib to show husband-and-wife union; initial state included dominion over creatures and immunity from suffering and death until disobedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: God's command to Adam and Eve as a test of obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: To try their obedience God commanded Adam and Eve not to eat of a certain fruit which grew in the garden of Paradise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The command was simple and intended as a test of obedience and of their regard for authority rather than the intrinsic difficulty of the prohibition; obedience in small things signals faithfulness in greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of the Fall (effects on humanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam and Eve on account of their sin lost innocence and holiness, and were doomed to sickness and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains concrete consequences: loss of grace and friendship with God, bodily rebellion against the soul, suffering, toil, mortality, and loss of Heaven for Adam and his posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original Sin: definition and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The sin which we inherit from our first parents is called Original Sin. This sin is called original because it comes down to us from our first parents, and we are brought into the world with its guilt on our souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Original Sin can be forgiven (e.g., by baptism), the corruption of nature and other punishments remain (concupiscence) so that we must merit by overcoming temptations and be kept humble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaculate Conception of Mary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blessed Virgin Mary ... was preserved free from the guilt of Original Sin, and this privilege is called her Immaculate Conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason given: as Mother of God it would not be fitting for her even momentarily to be subject to the devil; she was preserved through the merits of her divine Son and can aid Christians in temptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocation: existence, importance, and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: God assigned to everyone in this world a certain work to perform in a particular state of life, and this work is called 'vocation.' ... The signs of our vocation are, therefore, as stated: first, a strong desire, and second, an aptitude for the state to which we believe we are called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To discover vocation: pray for guidance, ask your confessor's advice, consider constant inclination and ability to fulfill duties (aptitude of mind, soul, or body). Do not enter a state not to which you are called out of parental pressure or selfish reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual sin: definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual sin is any willful thought, word, deed, or omission contrary to the law of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be sinful these must be willful (full knowledge and freedom) and contrary to God's law (or law of His Church). Sins of omission (not doing what is commanded) are as real as sins of commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of actual sin: mortal and venial
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of actual sin--mortal and venial. 'Mortal' ... kills the soul. 'Venial' sin does not drive out all the grace; it wounds the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes severity and spiritual effect: mortal sin deprives sanctifying grace and brings everlasting death; venial sin lessens grace and makes one more susceptible to mortal sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions necessary for a sin to be mortal
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a sin mortal three things are necessary: a grievous matter, sufficient reflection, and full consent of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stealing a pin lacks 'grievous matter'; stealing a valuable jewel is grievous. 'Sufficient reflection' means knowing what one is doing; 'full consent' means acting freely and willfully (accidents or lack of will remove culpability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venial sin: definition and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Venial sin is a slight offense against the law of God in matters of less importance, or in matters of great importance it is an offense committed without sufficient reflection or full consent of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects include lessening of the love of God, making us less worthy of His help, and weakening the power to resist mortal sin. Frequent venial sin can lead to mortal sin by degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinfulness depends on knowledge and intention (material vs formal sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If what we do is not known to be a sin while we do it, it is no sin for us ... On the other hand, if the person, thinking it was Friday when it was really Thursday, ate meat, knowing it to be forbidden, that person would commit a mortal sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'material' sin (would be sinful if knowledge were present) from actual culpable sin; once one knows an act is wrong, repeating it incurs guilt. Avoid judging others who may lack the same knowledge; better to instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt seek instruction from competent authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When, therefore, we have such a doubt we must seek information from those who can enlighten us on the subject, so that we may act without the danger of sinning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel: consult confessors or those able to clarify the law; do not fall into scrupulosity, but obtain reasoned guidance to act safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral duty: must do good, not merely avoid harm
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to simply do no harm, we must also do some good. Heaven is a reward, and we must do something to merit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: an office boy who 'did no harm' but neglected assigned work does not deserve wages. Similarly, Christians must perform the works God requires in their vocation rather than be passive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief sources of sin: the seven capital sins
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief sources of sin are seven: Pride, Covetousness, Lust, Anger, Gluttony, Envy, and Sloth; and they are commonly called capital sins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each capital sin acts as a 'source' that gathers other sins; one person's 'predominant sin' should be discovered and combated, for removing the root will help destroy subordinate sins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride (capital sin): definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pride' is an inordinate self-esteem. Pride comes under the First Commandment; because by thinking too much of ourselves we neglect God, and give to ourselves the honor due to Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Followers of pride include conceit, hypocrisy, foolish display in dress or conduct, harshness to others, waste of time on ourselves. Warnings about vanity of worldly goods and transient nature of beauty and wealth are given as antidotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covetousness (avarice): definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Covetousness,' the same as avarice, greed, etc., is an inordinate desire for worldly goods. 'Inordinate,' because it is not avarice to prudently provide for the future either for ourselves or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covetousness comes under the Tenth Commandment; followers include want of charity, dishonest dealing, theft. The virtue required is contentment with what one has obtained honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lust (capital sin): definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lust' is the desire for sins of the flesh; for impure thoughts, words, or actions. It comes under the Sixth and Ninth Commandments, and includes all that is forbidden by those Commandments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lust and impurity cover habitual desire to violate sexual commandments; placed alongside other capital sins as a principal source that leads to many subordinate sins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prayer and vigilance to resist temptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Lord once cautioned His Apostles (Matt. 26:41) to watch and pray lest they fall into temptation; teaching us also by the same warning that, besides praying against our spiritual enemies, we must watch their maneuvers and be ever ready to repel their attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: maintain vigilance and prayer; seek heavenly assistance (e.g., Blessed Virgin) and avoid dangerous occasions of sin ('do not go into the dangerous occasion') to prevent falling into temptation.
